overview: Samoa has a long history of Pacific voyaging, skilled craft and family-based social institutions. This card follows the western islands through colonial government and independence, with clearly identified earlier background. Samoan people and culture also extend to American Samoa and overseas communities; the modern state is not the whole Samoan world.

periods.title: Colonial partition and German administration
periods.summary: Britain, Germany and the United States agreed to divide the archipelago in December 1899 without consulting Samoans. The western islands came under German rule, while the eastern islands followed a separate political history.

periods.title: New Zealand rule and the struggle for independence
periods.summary: New Zealand occupied the western islands in 1914. Epidemic catastrophe and opposition to colonial rule shaped this period, including the Mau movement and the long campaign for self-government.

periods.title: An independent Samoa
periods.summary: Western Samoa regained independence on 1 January 1962. Family networks, language and cultural institutions continued to connect the islands with Samoan communities overseas.

items.text: Pottery fragments recovered during construction of the Mulifanua ferry berth on Upolu in 1973 included the tooth-stamped decoration associated with Lapita. Their context links the islands to a much older Pacific settlement history, long before the modern state.

A 2001 radiocarbon study placed occupation of the Mulifanua site around 930 to 800 BCE. These are calibrated estimates for a particular archaeological site, not an exact founding date for Samoa or a date assigned from a later genealogy.

A Samoan tattooing implement in Te Papa combines a bone comb, turtle-shell plate and wooden handle. A mallet drives the toothed edge, while combs of different widths make broad areas or fine lines. The object makes the precision of the tattooist's craft visible.

Ie Samoa fine mats are woven from narrow pandanus strips and finished with feathers and fringe. Preparing and weaving such fine material takes sustained skill and labor; the mats are valued for workmanship and the histories they acquire through exchange.

Fine mats circulate at weddings, funerals and other gatherings, reaffirming relationships between families. Village committees and master weavers teach the practice, making production a form of shared knowledge as well as individual artistry.

The aiga, or extended family, connects daily life with service, respect and reciprocal care. Family members exchange food, money and practical support, including across national borders. These obligations are lived and debated differently by different generations.

Matai titles, genealogies, language and ceremonial responsibilities are parts of fa'asamoa. Together they organize belonging and public relationships; the term does not describe an identical way of life for every Samoan household.

Christian teaching introduced by John Williams in 1830 became part of a changing religious landscape. Samoan forms of church life developed in close relationship with fa'asamoa, rather than simply replacing every earlier social institution.

The arrival of the influenza-infected Talune in 1918 led to a devastating epidemic under New Zealand administration. The disaster affected families and food production, making colonial governance part of everyday experience as well as constitutional history.

The Mau pursued self-government through organized, nonviolent resistance. In December 1929, colonial police killed peaceful demonstrators, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. The movement's history records Samoan political action, not merely a transfer between foreign rulers.
In 1936 New Zealand recognized the Mau as a legitimate political organization and repealed the Samoan Offenders Ordinance. Independence still required a longer struggle and arrived on 1 January 1962.

Samoan language nests and school programs in New Zealand connect language learning with shared leadership and cultural knowledge. These institutions show how communities maintain and reshape connections to Samoa across generations of migration.

ending.text: Colonial administration of Western Samoa ended with independence on 1 January 1962. Samoan communities, chiefly institutions and cultural practices continue in the independent state, American Samoa and the diaspora. A last map observation is not the end of the people or their history.
